source.title: High-dimensional networks and mean squared error for possibly misspecified models

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test MSE across model sizes and argues that the interpolation peak can be an artifact of the ridge parameter, reporting that it disappears with cross-validated tuning.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-MSE sweeps for simulated ridge regression, which bear on the general double-descent and regularization versions. It does not test deep networks, training epochs, or sample-size sweeps. Cited results from other work and the paper's neighborhood-selection outcomes are not rows because they do not measure the claim's test-error behavior.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own simulated ridge-regression sweeps of test MSE against p/n. It shows a peak at p = n followed by a second descent at near-zero ridge, and argues the peak is an artifact that vanishes with cross-validated ridge. That bears on V4 (a non-deep model class) and V6 (dependence on regularization). Its main topic is neighbourhood selection, but these MSE results are its own. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors say the interpolation peak in their ridge example is an artifact of a poorly chosen (near-zero) ridge parameter that disappears with cross-validated alpha. With a correct linear model the test-MSE minimum stays at the true model; under misspecification it can shift to a highly overparameterized model. Their main conclusion, beyond the record's paraphrase, is that MDL with a volume penalty gives the correct or smaller neighbourhood (low false positives) in high dimensions, and they recommend it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses simulated nodewise linear regression with ridge estimation and predictor-count sweeps, rather than testing deep-network scaling as in the original claim sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported peak depends on ridge-parameter choice: it appears with fixed α = 0.0001 and disappears with α selected by 10-fold cross-validation.
record.problems: The simulations use n = 40 total observations, with ntrain = 32 and ntest = 8. No uncertainty estimates or number of simulation repetitions are stated in the supplied text. Much of the curve evidence is described qualitatively rather than reported as numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Neighborhood-selection and false-positive-rate results were left out because they do not measure test-error curves. Cited results from prior studies were also excluded.

untested.parts: No deep networks; linear ridge regression only.
No sweep over training sample size; n is fixed at 40.
Only linear/ridge regression in simulation; no other model classes or real data.
Effective df is defined (Sec. 5.1) but not used to predict peak location on any axis.
Label-noise dependence not varied (SNR fixed at 2). No multiple or triple peaks examined. Optimality of the tuned ridge not established.
Test MSE is never plotted against effective degrees of freedom.

missing.what: Lasso with CV-chosen penalty shows no interpolation peak but generally higher test MSE than ridge. This bears on regularization removing the peak.
missing.locator: Sec. 4; Appendix H, Fig. H.1 bottom row

missing.what: Bias-variance decomposition: test variance rises toward p = n and falls after it; the peak is attributed to variance controlled by alpha.
missing.locator: Sec. 3, Fig. 3(b); Sec. 4 (Lemma B.3); Fig. H.1 right column

record.verdict_notes: Single-author Journal of Mathematical Psychology-style paper whose double-descent evidence is a small simulation: n = 40, ntrain = 32, ntest = 8. The number of replications is not stated and no uncertainty is reported. The alpha values are inconsistent: 0.0001 in Sec. 4 and Fig. H.1, but 0.5 in the Appendix H text. Neighbourhood-selection and false-positive results are correctly excluded from the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No deep networks are tested; the simulations use linear regression with ridge estimation.
No sweep over training epochs or training time.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
Tests simulated linear-regression settings only, not a range of model classes.
The paper defines effective degrees of freedom but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across axes.
Tests whether ridge-parameter tuning changes the peak; does not test whether label noise or variance causes it, multiple or triple peaks, or optimality of the tuning.
Does not measure the curve against an effective-parameter count or show that this converts double descent into an ordinary U-shape.

rows.subject: linear regression estimated with ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of predictors and measured test MSE with fixed ridge parameter α = 0.0001.
rows.measure: Test MSE as a function of model size
rows.value: The paper describes a peak at the interpolation point followed by a second descent.
rows.locator: Section 3, Figure 3; Appendix H, Figure H.1
rows.note: The paper identifies the Figure 3 peak as occurring with the fixed α = 0.0001 setting.
rows.check: State is correct but rests on qualitative description only; no curve values. Sec. 4 and the Fig. H.1 caption give alpha = 0.0001, while Appendix H says the ridge was fit with alpha = 0.5 or by CV. Note this inconsistency.

rows.subject: linear regression estimated with ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number of predictors and measured test MSE with α selected by 10-fold cross-validation.
rows.measure: Test MSE as a function of model size
rows.value: The paper states that the peak disappears with a carefully selected ridge parameter.
rows.note: The cross-validated α is selected using the smallest MSE; the paper does not give numerical curve values.
rows.check: 'Absent' refers to the interpolation peak. For V6 this is the predicted outcome (the peak disappears under tuned regularization), so it supports V6. For V4 it is a qualification, not a challenge: V4 does not claim the peak survives tuned regularization. Also, CV picks alpha by validation MSE, not provably the optimum, and no numbers are given.

rows.subject: linear regression estimated with ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of predictors and measured test MSE.
rows.baseline: The correct neighborhood size, p = 5, at p/n ≈ 0.15
rows.value: The global minimum of test MSE remains at the correct model size, p = 5; the paper says test MSE at the correct neighborhood size is optimal.
rows.note: The stated minimum does not specify whether test MSE has the fall-rise-fall shape.
rows.check: The ridge alpha used for Fig. 4 is not stated, and the curve's shape between p/n = 1 and 10 is not described numerically. Only the location of the global minimum is stated, at the correct model p = 5.

conditions.value: sigmoid conditional mean, estimated with a linear model

rows.baseline: Test MSE 0.0877 at the correct neighborhood size p = 5
rows.value: Test MSE 0.0844 at p/n = 10 (p = 320); the paper says the global minimum shifts to this largest model.
rows.note: The high-dimensional model's reported test MSE is below the value at the correct neighborhood size.
rows.check: The gain is small (0.0844 vs 0.0877), with ntest = 8. No repetitions or uncertainty are stated, and the alpha used is not stated.

relationships.condition: Ridge with near-zero alpha (0.0001), correctly specified linear model, p/n 0.1 to 2
relationships.reason: Test MSE peaks at p = n, then descends again (Fig. 3a) (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE peaked at p = n and then declined again.

relationships.condition: Misspecified sigmoid data fit with a linear model, p/n up to 10
relationships.reason: Test MSE at p = 320 (0.0844) is below that at the correct p = 5 (0.0877). The margin is small and has no uncertainty (r4).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE was 0.0844 at p = 320 versus 0.0877 at the correct p = 5, a small difference without uncertainty estimates.

relationships.reason: The interpolation peak disappears with tuned alpha, so the shape depends on the regularization choice (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Tuning ridge alpha with 10-fold cross-validation removed the interpolation peak.

relationships.condition: Near-zero alpha versus CV-tuned alpha, linear ridge simulation
relationships.reason: The peak appears at alpha = 0.0001 and disappears with CV-tuned alpha (Fig. H.1) (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: The peak appeared at α=0.0001 and disappeared when α was selected by cross-validation.
